title: Seven Years Like a Few Days — the Well's Mouth, the Switch, the Sons
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. We closed the last lesson at Bethel: a man on the run lay down with a stone under his head and fell asleep, heaven opened over him, and God said, "Behold, I am with you." Today he walks the rest of that road, all the way to the house of his uncle Laban.

And the question this lesson puts to us is one that everybody who has served for any length of time runs into: with the same piece of work in front of them, why does one person dry up after three years, while another is still shining after thirty?
The same overtime. The same caregiving. The same church service. The same marriage. For some people it grows lighter the longer they do it; for others it grows heavier.

Let me put the answer up front: love can turn seven years into a few days, and service without love will turn three years into thirty. But there is another half to this chapter — the woman nobody loved was seen by the One in heaven.
1. He Rolled That Stone Away by Himself

Verse 1: "Then Jacob went on his journey, and came to the land of the children of the east." The Hebrew is וַיִּשָּׂא רַגְלָיו (*vayisa raglav*), literally "he lifted up his feet" — an idiom, and what it pictures is a man setting out with a light step.

Brothers and sisters, that detail is beautiful. In chapter 28 he walked until he could walk no further and dropped to the ground where he was; after that night at Bethel, his step has grown light. The same road of flight — but walking it before you have met God and walking it afterwards are not the same walk.
Verse 2: he sees a well out in the field, and three flocks of sheep lying there beside it, and — "The stone on the well's mouth was large."
And that stone on the well's mouth comes back four times over: verses 2, 3, 8 and 10. The writer keeps tugging at your sleeve. That stone is big.

Verse 3 gives us the custom: "There all the flocks were gathered. They rolled the stone from the well's mouth, and watered the sheep, and put the stone back on the well's mouth in its place." Which is to say — it took several men together to shift it.

Then verse 10: "When Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban, his mother's brother, and the sheep of Laban, his mother's brother, Jacob went near, and rolled the stone from the well's mouth, and watered the flock of Laban his mother's brother."
He pushed it away on his own.

Brothers and sisters, the text never explains where the strength came from. Some people say it was the strength of love, and I do not think that is entirely a joke — for the sake of one particular person, a man can lift what he could not ordinarily lift.

And notice one thing: the first thing he does is not to introduce himself. It is to serve. He rolls the stone away first, waters the flock first, and only then does the text say, "Jacob kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice, and wept."

There is one more detail. In verse 4, the first words out of his mouth to those complete strangers are, "My relatives, where are you from?" The Hebrew there is אַחַי (*achai*) — "my brothers." A man on the run, and the moment he opens his mouth he is claiming kin. He is looking for somewhere he can belong.
Why does the text bother to tell us that Jacob rolled that great stone off the well's mouth by himself?

Verse 2 says the stone on the well's mouth was large, and verse 3 says the custom was to wait until all the flocks had been gathered before rolling the stone away and watering the sheep — it took several men together to move it. Then verse 10 says Jacob went near and rolled the stone from the well's mouth: one man doing what it normally took a crowd to do. The text never explains where the strength came from. It simply sets the moment inside another moment — the moment he catches sight of Rachel. That detail is saying something very human: when a person is moved by love, the strength in him is of a different order. And it also plants a seed for later — that same strength goes into twenty years of hard labour, and into that one night at the ford of the Jabbok.
He kissed her and wept out loud the moment they met. Was that improper in that culture?

In the ancient Near East, kissing a relative on the cheek when you met was ordinary courtesy, so the gesture itself is not strange. What is strange is the weeping out loud — a grown man sobbing in public. Remember where he is: he has fled several hundred kilometres alone, he owns nothing, and he has no idea how his uncle is going to treat him. In the moment he sees a relative, twenty-odd days of held-in tension come pouring out of him. And that is very practical for us: after a long stretch of strain, a person meets one small kindness and falls apart — that is not fragility, that is the body telling the truth. So if somebody beside you suddenly weeps in front of you, do not rush to comfort him and do not rush to analyse him. Let him finish crying first.
2. A Light from the Original: Love Makes Seven Years Feel Like a Few Days
Verse 18: "Jacob loved Rachel. He said, 'I will serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter.'"
And verse 20 is the most famous sentence in this chapter — possibly in the whole book of Genesis:
"Jacob served seven years for Rachel. They seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her."
Brothers and sisters, read that one slowly, because it is very easily read as a romantic line to be embroidered on a cushion — and then its real weight goes straight past you.
The text does not say those seven years were short. What the text says is this: because he loved her deeply, those seven years looked to him like a few days.

The seven years were exactly as long as seven years. And we know how hard they were — in chapter 31, verse 40, he says it himself: "This was my situation: in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep fled from my eyes."
Not one gram of the objective hardship was taken away. What changed is that there was somebody in his heart.
Brothers and sisters, for anybody who serves, this lands like a blow.

Why is one person still shining after thirty years of service? Not because his ministry happens to be lighter, but because there is Someone in his heart who is worth it. And why does another dry out after three years? Also not because his ministry is unusually heavy, but because the One in his heart has gone missing, and all that is left is duty, face, and invitations he was too embarrassed to turn down.

In Revelation chapter 2, the Lord Jesus says to the church in Ephesus, "I know your works, and your toil and perseverance … You have perseverance and have endured for my name's sake, and have not grown weary. But I have this against you, that you left your first love."
Brothers and sisters, in that church everything was right. Only one thing had gone missing. And that one thing is precisely the thing that makes seven years feel like a few days.
"Jacob served seven years for Rachel. They seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her." Is that not a rather romantic way of talking about love?

The text really is written beautifully, but you have to put it back into its context: after those seven years came the switch, then another seven, then another six — twenty years in all, and the text has him saying, "in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep fled from my eyes." So "but a few days" is not saying that those seven years were light work. It is saying that when there is hope inside the waiting, the felt length of the waiting is different. And the reminder for us is this: love does not make the cost disappear; love changes the weight of the cost. The reverse holds too — one year of waiting with no hope in it feels like ten. So the question to ask is this: the thing I am waiting for — do I still believe it is coming?
3. In the Morning, Behold, It Was Leah
Verse 21. The seven years are up, and he says, "Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her."
Verse 23: "In the evening, he took Leah his daughter, and brought her to Jacob. He went in to her."
Verse 25: "In the morning, behold, it was Leah! He said to Laban, 'What is this you have done to me? Didn't I serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?'"
Brothers and sisters — "Why then have you deceived me?" That sentence, coming out of Jacob's mouth, is by itself the largest irony in the chapter.
And Laban's answer is one of the sharpest sentences in the whole Bible: "It is not done so in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn."

Brothers and sisters, two chapters ago a younger son put on his elder brother's clothes, strapped goatskins onto his hands and passed himself off as the firstborn in order to deceive a father who could not see. And now, in a bridal chamber where nothing at all can be seen, an elder daughter has been put in the place of a younger one.
He deceived with a borrowed birthright; now he has been switched with a firstborn daughter.
He traded on his father's failing eyes; now he has been blindfolded by the dark.
And in the moment Laban says those two words — the elder, the younger — that is the knife going in.
Galatians 6:7 says, "Don't be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap."

But brothers and sisters, I want to draw a very important distinction here: this is discipline, not revenge. Hebrews 12:6 says, "for whom the Lord loves, he disciplines." Discipline exists in order to change somebody; revenge exists in order to get even. God spent twenty years prising open that grasping hand — and the name Jacob means exactly that: the one who grabs the heel.
Laban switched Leah in on him. Why does the text report a deception like that so calmly?

The force of Hebrew narrative usually lies in the juxtaposition, not in the commentary. The original of verse 25 is very visual: "In the morning, behold, it was Leah!" That "behold" is Jacob's own point of view. And what makes the back of your neck go cold is Laban's reason: "It is not done so in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn" — the elder, and the younger. In chapter 27 Jacob took advantage of a father whose eyes were failing and passed himself off as the elder; now, in the dark, somebody has swapped the elder in for the younger. The text does not need to comment. The reader recognises the mirror for himself. That is recompense told as a story, not a lesson in revenge.
After he had been cheated, why did Jacob not lose his temper and walk out?

All the text records is one question — "Why then have you deceived me?" — and then he accepts the terms and serves another seven years. There are several likely reasons: he is in a foreign country with nothing in his pocket; the one he wants is Rachel; and he has himself just finished deceiving somebody, so he cannot work up much righteous indignation. The text does not offer an explanation on his behalf, but that quietness is worth looking at — a man who has once used tricks tends to have nothing to say when tricks are used on him. And there is a very honest reminder in that for us: what we are least able to argue back against is usually the very thing we ourselves have done. So deal with the debts of the past, or they will strike you dumb at the least convenient moment.
4. Yahweh Saw That Leah Was Hated
Verse 30: "He went in also to Rachel, and he loved also Rachel more than Leah, and served with him seven more years."
And then verse 31: "Yahweh saw that Leah was hated, and he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren."
Brothers and sisters, look at the subject and the verb of that sentence. Yahweh. Saw.
Where the English says Leah was "hated", the Hebrew is literally that: the hated one. It is a very heavy word — it is the word the law uses of the wife who is not loved (Deuteronomy 21:15).

And in the whole chapter, not one person speaks up for her. Her father treated her as a bargaining chip and sent her in; her husband loves her sister; and her sister will be in competition with her for the rest of her life.
In this household where nobody sees her, the text says: Yahweh saw.
And the four names that come next are the most moving passage in the chapter.
The first son is called Reuben, and she says, "Because Yahweh has looked at my affliction; for now my husband will love me."
The second is called Simeon, and she says, "Because Yahweh has heard that I am hated, he has therefore given me this son also."
The third is called Levi, and she says, "Now this time my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons."

Brothers and sisters, in every one of those first three names she is waiting for one man to turn round. He has seen my affliction — so now he will love me. He has heard that I am hated — so now he will give me one more glance. Three sons now — surely now he will be joined to me.
Three times. Three children. And that man never once turned round.
And then comes the fourth. Verse 35:
"She conceived again, and bore a son. She said, 'This time I will praise Yahweh.' Therefore she named him Judah."
Brothers and sisters, this time she does not mention her husband at all.
She no longer says "now he will love me", or "now he will be joined to me." She says: this time I will praise Yahweh.
And that name — Judah, יְהוּדָה (*Yehudah*) — has "praise" for its root.

Hold on to this: of the twelve tribes, the royal tribe is Judah. David comes out of Judah. And Matthew opens his Gospel with "Judah became the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar" — and from there the line runs on, all the way down to Jesus Christ.
That woman nobody loved — the child she bore in the very moment she finally lifted her eyes off her husband became an ancestor of the Messiah.
And there is one light sentence at the end of verse 35: "Then she stopped bearing." She came to rest here, at praise.
"Yahweh saw that Leah was hated, and he opened her womb" — why does God stand on the side of the one who is not loved?

The verb in verse 31 is "saw" (רָאָה) — the same root as in chapter 16, where Hagar says, "You are a God who sees." Scripture shows us again and again that God pays particular attention to the one nobody picked, the one left out in the cold, the one placed at the back of the line. And the names of Leah's four sons are a journey of the heart: Reuben (God has looked at my affliction), Simeon (God has heard that I am hated), Levi (now my husband will be joined to me), Judah (this time I will praise Yahweh). The first three are all hoping her husband will turn round; with the fourth she stops asking for a human response at all, and turns to God. And the line that runs to the Messiah comes down through that fourth one.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching "the seven years seemed like a few days" as a romantic line about being in love. What that verse is really about is the staying power that love supplies, and it applies to marriage, yes, but also to service, to caregiving, to sitting with somebody. If all you preach is the romance, the congregation goes home feeling warm and has never once been challenged to examine where its own fuel is coming from.

The second is preaching Leah as a supporting character or a villain. The Messiah comes out of her son Judah; Genesis 49:31 says she was buried in the cave of Machpelah, together with Abraham and Sarah, with Isaac and Rebekah — while Rachel was buried on the road to Ephrath. How highly God thinks of her could hardly be plainer. If you belittle her, you will wound every person in the room who has ever felt like the spare.

The third is using this chapter to justify polygamy, or family chaos in general. The text is describing, not prescribing. And the whole of chapter 30 — the rivalry — and chapter 37 — brother turning on brother — are the consequences of exactly this. In the whole of Genesis, there is not one household with more than one wife that is at peace.

The fourth is preaching Laban's deception as God taking revenge on Jacob. This is discipline, not revenge. Preach it as payback and your congregation will live in a kind of dread — as though God kept a ledger and were waiting for the chance to settle up.

The fifth is preaching Jacob's seven years only as "he loved her so much", and never mentioning how passive he is throughout the whole affair. He does love Rachel, that is true. But by the end of chapter 29 there are two wives in his house; by the beginning of chapter 30 there are four women. He never once actually deals with the disorder in that family; he simply keeps walking forward. Loving one person is no substitute for governing a household.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: I have served in the church for many years and I am more and more tired, more and more as though I were paying off a debt — what should I do? Brothers and sisters, this chapter hands you a very accurate diagnostic tool, and it is verse 20. Ask yourself one question: does this thing look to me like seven years passing as a few days, or like a few days dragging on as seven years? If it is the second, then most likely it is not a ministry problem. It is a fuel problem. And I want to give you three directions. First, go back and find him again. Revelation 2:5 says, "Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works." Not try twice as hard — remember. Second, check who you are doing it for. Jacob served seven years with one particular person in his eye. Who is in your eye when you serve? If all that is left is the structures, the reports and the people you were too polite to refuse, then you will dry out. Third — and this needs saying honestly too — some exhaustion is not a spiritual problem, it is a load problem. Seven years is long, and he really was worn out; he says it himself: in the day the drought consumed him, and the frost by night. Admitting that you are tired is not unspiritual.

The second question: at home I am the child who is not the favourite; or in my marriage I am the one who keeps giving and is never treasured — what does this chapter say to me? Brothers and sisters, there is one sentence in this chapter written specifically for you: "Yahweh saw that Leah was hated." I want to say three things. First, your situation is real, and the text does not water it down. It uses a very heavy word — hated. God does not say, "Actually, you are imagining it." Second, God saw, and God did something. He did not change Jacob's heart — from beginning to end the text never records that Jacob later came to love Leah. What he did was give her something else. Sometimes God's answer is not to change that person; it is to do a different work in you. Third, and most important of all: her turning point is not her husband turning round. It is that she herself took her eyes off him. The first three names are all waiting for a man to come back; the fourth name says, "This time I will praise Yahweh" — and that child walked into the family tree of the Lord Jesus. Brothers and sisters, staking your happiness on whether one person turns round is the most exhausting way there is to live. That "this time" — when is your turn to say it?
In a position where I am not valued, how do I keep going?

Leah gives us three very practical moves. First, say the hurt out loud: the names she gave her children were her diary, and she never pretended she was fine. Second, do not stake the whole weight on the person who will not turn round — the first three names were all hoping in her husband, and that made the waiting more bitter the longer it went on. Third, find one thing you can turn towards God with: by the time she reaches Judah she says, "This time I will praise Yahweh", and in that moment her centre of gravity changes. In practical terms you can do this: write one true sentence to God every day, and find one person who knows what your situation is. And if that position involves long-term belittling and harm, then take seriously the possibility of adjusting it or leaving it.
7. Living 321 Out — Someone Worth It First, Then the Staying Power
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Jacob rolled that great stone off the well's mouth by himself. And in John chapter 4, the Lord Jesus sits down by Jacob's well and says to a Samaritan woman, "whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life." Brothers and sisters, my role model is this: he rolls the stone away for people with his own hands — and the last stone he rolled away was the one at the mouth of a tomb.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter lets us see that "whatever a man sows, that he will also reap" is not a curse but a law, one that has been written into the shape of a story. The standard is not only in the commandments; it is in the architecture of the narrative. The writer does not have to preach at us. All he has to do is let Laban say those two words: the elder, the younger.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — verse 31 says, "Yahweh saw." Brothers and sisters, one of the things the Holy Spirit does most often is to let the person nobody sees know that she is seen. If some name surfaces in your mind this week — somebody you have not been in touch with for a long time, somebody nobody pays any attention to — that may very well not be a random thought.

Let Jesus be King — Laban changed Jacob's wages ten times and cheated him once over a marriage, and the text never records him taking revenge. God spent twenty years prising open that grasping hand. Letting Jesus be King includes accepting his way of disciplining and his timing for it — and the way he uses is very often not the one we would have chosen.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — Leah says, "This time I will praise Yahweh." And the only place in the whole chapter where glory is genuinely given to God comes from the person with the least reason on earth to sing. Brothers and sisters, the truest worship usually does not come out of a season when everything is going well.

Establish God's system — the twelve tribes were born out of this broken family, and the Messiah comes from Leah's son Judah. Brothers and sisters, God's system is not built upon perfect households. Establishing God's system begins with the person God has seen — and that person is usually not the one in the family with the most to show for himself.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We are fond of saying "life first, then relationships, then ministry." And this chapter hands us a very concrete example of the reverse. Jacob's ministry capacity is formidable — he can shift by himself a stone that normally takes a crowd, he can shepherd enormous flocks, he can build up an estate over twenty years. And his household is a mess the whole time, and that mess finally catches fire in chapter 37, when his sons sell their own brother. So remember this: ability can cover disorder for a very long time, but it cannot cover it for a lifetime. If life and relationships go untreated, then the bigger the ministry grows, the bigger the bill grows with it.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Well
Brothers and sisters, the same well and the same wedding, falling into four different hearts, are not seen in the same way at all.

The proud heart says, "Jacob had it coming." What most satisfies a heart like this, when it finishes the chapter, is watching a bad man get what was owed to him. Brothers and sisters, look at the posture of the text — it does not gloat. It simply records Laban's sentence about the elder and the younger. And the better question is this: what am I sowing?

The fearful heart says, "Then the things I did in the past — will they come back on me too?" To a heart like that I want to say: discipline is not the same thing as revenge. God disciplined Jacob, and in the same breath, back in chapter 28, said to him, "I will not leave you until I have done that which I have spoken of to you." He disciplines with one hand and holds you up with the other. And Hebrews 12:11 says that discipline "afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it."

The ashamed heart says, "I am Leah." It may be that all your life you have been the one who was not chosen, the one nobody saw, the one brought in to make up the numbers. Brothers and sisters, read verse 31 out loud: "Yahweh saw that Leah was hated." The subject of that sentence is Yahweh. Not one person in that household spoke up for her — and the Bible wrote this sentence down on her behalf.

The wounded heart says, "I waited that long, and he still never turned round." You may already have done what Leah did — waited three times, five times, ten years. Brothers and sisters, I am not going to tell you "just wait one more time." What I want to point you to is the fourth name. Her way out was not that her husband finally came back. It was that she herself said one sentence: this time I will praise Yahweh. That is not giving up. That is moving the weight off a person who cannot carry it, and onto a God who can.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, take a measurement of your staying power. Pick one thing you are currently doing and ask yourself honestly: does this look to me like seven years passing as a few days, or like a few days dragging on as seven years? Write the answer down.
Second, remember the beginning. If the answer was the second one, spend twenty minutes this week remembering: why did I start doing this in the first place? Who was the One in my heart back then?
Third, say a word on behalf of a "Leah". Think about who around you is the person who keeps doing the work and is never mentioned. Thank him once this week, concretely — and say his name out loud.

Fourth, say "this time I will praise Yahweh" once. Find one thing you have been waiting on some person to respond to, hand it over this week, and give thanks to God for it once — not because it has come through, but because God has seen.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences. There is a man in the Bible who worked seven years in order to marry a woman, and the Bible says that because he loved her deeply, he saw those seven years as a few days — the seven years did not get shorter, love made them feel shorter. In the same chapter there is another woman, never loved by her husband, who bore three children, and every time she named one she was hoping her husband would turn round. And then came the fourth, and she said, "This time I will praise Yahweh" — and the descendant of that child is Jesus.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that the staying power of my service does not lie in my willpower, but in the One in my heart who is worth it.
I declare that I will go back to my first love, and not simply try twice as hard.
I declare that I will not stake my happiness on whether one person turns round.
I declare that I will say that sentence out loud: this time I will praise Yahweh.
This week I am supposed to do something for a person who has been left out in the cold — but I am the one who has been left out. What then?

Then catch yourself first, and go and look at other people afterwards; the two do not conflict. Step one: say your situation out loud honestly — to God, and to one person you trust; do not use service to paper over it. Step two: do one very small kind thing for somebody else, because a person who has been overlooked falls very easily into a loop where nobody is left but himself, and putting a hand out breaks the loop. Step three: remember Leah's fourth child — your worth is not decided by the person who will not look at you. And if you are in an environment where you are belittled over the long term, talk to a pastor, and consider seeking professional help as well.
Brothers and sisters, if only two sentences from this lesson may remain, I want to set them side by side.
The first is verse 20: "They seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her."
The second is verse 35: "This time I will praise Yahweh."
One is about the staying power of love. The other is about how a person who is not loved goes on living.
And put together, those two sentences are exactly the whole of what this chapter has to give us.

If you are holding on inside something hard right now, the first sentence asks you: is the One in your heart still there? If he is gone, that is not because you have not tried hard enough. It is that you need to go back and find him.

If you are inside a relationship where you are not treasured, the second sentence tells you: there is One who has seen. And your way out is not to wait for that person to turn round. It is to move your eyes onto the Lord who has been looking at you all along.
Brothers and sisters, remember the quietest sentence in this chapter: "Yahweh saw that Leah was hated."
There is no miracle in that sentence, no thunder, no angel. Only one verb: saw.
And that one seeing brought forth Judah in the end, and brought forth David, and brought forth the One born in Bethlehem.

The focus is not on who loves me, not on whether anybody notices my service, and not on whether that person will ever turn round. The focus is on Jesus — he is the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the flower that opened on the line that came from the woman nobody loved. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to come back to our first love, and to say out loud the name of one person nobody ever mentions. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ "The elder" and "the younger" — Laban's reason happens to hold up a mirror to exactly what Jacob did in chapter 27. The text uses juxtaposition instead of commentary. Why is that more powerful?
2. ★★★ "They seemed to him but a few days" — love does not make the cost disappear, love changes the weight of the cost. How would you apply that sentence to the thing you are waiting for right now?
3. ★ The names of Leah's four sons are a journey of the heart. Between the third and the fourth, what did she swap out?
4. ★★ "Yahweh saw that Leah was hated" — why does God pay particular attention to the one nobody picked?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I can shift it if I put my back into it), fearful (I am afraid it will never come), ashamed (I am the one who got swapped out), wounded (my own people cheated me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Yahweh saw that Leah was hated, and he opened her womb." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a relationship in which you have been "waiting for one person to turn round"? How much of your weight have you staked on him?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The person I most want to be seen by is …"
9. ★★ This week, which one thing will you do that shifts your centre of gravity towards God? Say it very concretely.

Leader's reminder: question nine will touch losses in marriage and in family. Do not let anyone in the group pass comment on anybody else's spouse or family members. If someone speaks about being belittled over a long period, follow up with him privately after the meeting and help him find support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, who is the "Leah" — the one who is always placed at the back? What will you do for that person this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work, or in your service, whose name gets left out most often?
12. ★★★ The one-true-sentence-a-day practice: this week, write one true sentence to God every day, unpolished. Say where you will write it, and when.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a woman in the Bible whose husband left her out in the cold all her life, and she wrote how she felt into the names of four children. Second, by the fourth she said, "This time I will praise Yahweh", and stopped waiting for her husband to turn round. Third, the king and the Saviour who came later came down from that fourth child. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the "Leah" you are going to care for this week, and the one thing you are going to do that turns you towards God. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord not to let us stake the weight of a whole life on a person who will not turn round.
